title: Motion Synthesis from Annotations
summary: Uses annotated action timelines and multiscale dynamic programming to assemble motion, including overlapping qualitative constraints.
limitations: Cannot invent frames or transitions absent from the database. Incompatible requirements trade annotation satisfaction against continuity, and smoothing may change duration. Painted labels do not supply unseen contact geometry or physical execution.
method: SVM-assisted labeling propagates sparse manual action annotations. Multiscale dynamic programming then selects motion blocks that match a requested timeline while minimizing discontinuity, followed by finer boundary and motion refinement.
conditions: User-painted positive, negative or unconstrained action labels on a timeline, plus optional timed pose, root-position and orientation constraints. Vocabulary is chosen by the animator rather than fixed natural-language task understanding.
evaluation: Sections 3–6 demonstrate combinations such as running with jumping or waving and enforced key poses. Coarse-to-fine optimization improves solutions interactively; examples test overlapping qualitative requirements rather than a controlled statistical generalization benchmark.
data_split: Uses a small annotated motion database, approximately seven minutes in the reported annotation exercise. SVM annotation propagation uses a manually labeled subset with interactive corrections. No held-out actor/action-combination benchmark or train/test percentage is reported for synthesis.
metrics: Annotation matching and motion-continuity objectives, interactive synthesis behavior, visual naturalness and low-level constraint satisfaction. Annotation speed is demonstrated; no standardized distributional generation or independent physics metric is reported.
evidence_locator: Sections 2–3 (annotations/synthesis), 4–5 (search/smoothing), 6 (Results); Figures 1, 5–7.
full_text_version: Proceedings/author PDF as retrieved 2026-11-19; no printed own-paper arXiv version found.

title: Multi-Track Timeline Control for Text-Driven 3D Human Motion Generation
summary: Test-time spatial stitching and temporal score arithmetic operate at every diffusion step.
method: Preprocesses prompts into per-body-part timelines; denoises local crops and combines corresponding pose components repeatedly during sampling.
conditions: Multiple texts with explicit time intervals and body-part assignments, supplied manually or inferred with GPT-3. Compatible overlapping part responsibilities are required; the motion is jointly assembled at every denoising step.
evaluation: Table 1 compares single-text, single-track and multi-track sampling with several denoisers. A filtered pairwise human study evaluates one hundred motions for realism and instruction adherence. Improvements are evaluated separately for semantics and transitions, avoiding an aggregate claim of physical correctness. The composition procedure updates all local denoising crops repeatedly rather than stitching final outputs once.
limitations: Inherits base-model failures, unfamiliar stitched poses and imperfect timing. Incompatible parts remain problematic; long-motion TMR embeddings are unreliable, motivating cropped FID+. Contact mechanics and persistent object state are not modeled.
evidence_locator: Sections 3.1–3.4, 4.1–4.6; Table 1 and user-study protocol.
data_split: Backbone models train on HumanML3D. MDM-SMPL excludes HumanAct12 because pose parameters are unavailable. MTT is a manually designed evaluation-only timeline set with atomic text/source-motion references; no newly trained timeline partition or train/test percentage applies to STMC itself.
metrics: TMR R@1/R@3, motion-to-text M2T and motion-to-motion M2M similarity; FID+ uses five random five-second crops per generated timeline, and transition distance measures local consecutive-pose boundary jumps.
full_text_version: Proceedings/author PDF as retrieved 2026-11-19; no printed own-paper arXiv version found.

title: Seamless Human Motion Composition with Blended Positional Encodings
summary: FlowMDM generates temporally composed text-conditioned motion and evaluates transition quality.
limitations: Finite attention and independent low-frequency subsequence structure can limit distant action relationships. Good jerk or FID values do not establish semantic task prerequisites, foot-support correctness, scene collision freedom or object interaction dynamics.
method: Early denoising uses absolute positions for within-action structure; late denoising uses relative positions across boundaries. Pose-centric cross-attention associates each frame with its own condition.
conditions: Ordered text descriptions and durations, expanded to frame-specific conditions. Pose-centric cross-attention associates each frame with its own prompt while the denoising process changes positional-encoding regime.
evaluation: Tables 1–2 compare TEACH, DoubleTake, DiffCollage and MultiDiffusion with matched conditioning/positional choices. Thirty-one transitions between the thirty-two subsequences are evaluated separately; ablations examine positional blending, attention horizon and pose-centric conditioning. Extrapolation tests extend beyond training sequence durations.
data_split: Uses the standard BABEL and HumanML3D training/test divisions; exact partition proportions are not restated in Section 4.1. BABEL training may include consecutive annotated actions; HumanML3D lacks explicit transition annotations. Evaluation composes thirty-two sampled text-duration pairs per long sequence.
metrics: Subsequence R-Precision, matching distance, FID, diversity/multimodality; transition FID, Peak Jerk PJ and Area Under the Jerk AUJ quantify both abrupt spikes and excessive broad smoothing.
evidence_locator: Sections 3.1–3.3, 4.1–4.4; Tables 1–2; Eq. 4 for PJ/AUJ and supplementary evaluation details.

title: Human Motion Diffusion as a Generative Prior
summary: Introduces DoubleTake sequential composition, ComMDM two-person coordination and DiffusionBlending joint-control model composition.
limitations: DoubleTake needs overlap/refinement design; ComMDM needs interaction data and fine control requires extra training. These are distinct reuse mechanisms, not a universal zero-training composer. None guarantees physically valid contact or persistent object-state reasoning.
method: A frozen short-motion diffusion prior is reused for overlapping prompted intervals; a second take refines transitions. Separate small adapters or fine-tuned controlled priors support other composition modes.
conditions: DoubleTake consumes sequential prompts/durations with overlapping handshake regions. ComMDM additionally consumes interaction examples or a prefix; fine-tuned priors consume selected joint controls, and DiffusionBlending combines distinct control-conditioned predictions.
evaluation: Sequential evaluation constructs thirty-two-interval sequences and scores actions and boundaries separately. ComMDM completes three seconds from a one-second prefix and compares communication-layer placement. Fine-tuning and blending compare a common initial MDM against separately controlled models.
data_split: DoubleTake evaluates BABEL and HumanML3D; fine control uses HumanML3D test prompts/controls. ComMDM uses a small two-person dataset, including its ten-example few-shot setting. Exact aggregate train/test proportions are not restated and the three tasks should not be collapsed into one split.
metrics: Per-interval text-motion R-Precision/MM-Distance/FID/diversity, transition FID; ComMDM prefix completion reports root/joint L2 errors. Joint-control evaluation measures adherence and generation quality; qualitative studies assess blending.
evidence_locator: Sections 3.1–3.3, 4.1–4.3; Tables 1–3 and fine-control quantitative results.

title: FUSION: Full-Body Unified Motion Prior for Body and Hands via Diffusion
summary: Unifies body and hand datasets into a full-body motion prior, with optimization-driven object-motion and self-interaction applications.
limitations: Randomly combined hand/body motion lacks sequence-level semantic correlation. Fixed-grasp guidance limits contact changes, and the learned prior is not a text-plus-initial-state dynamic HOI generator. Body-only realism scores cannot validate dexterous hand or object dynamics.
method: Unconditional SMPL-X diffusion prior jointly models body/hands; task losses backpropagate through denoising to optimize noise. Local hand transfer preserves body wrists and filters additional penetration.
conditions: Unconditional whole-body/hand prior optimized for supplied keypoint tracks, object-motion trajectories or LLM-generated timed self-contact constraints. Object-guided synthesis assumes object motion and a stable grasp, so future interaction is partially prescribed.
evaluation: Keypoint control is compared with TLControl; hand/body ablations assess the benefit of unified training. Object-guided and self-interaction demonstrations optimize denoising noise with task losses. Human comparison separately assesses motion realism against HMP and captured motion.
evidence_locator: Sections 3.1–3.3, 4–5; Table 1; supplementary Sections 9–12 (metrics, ablations, self-contact).
data_split: Source pools include 145,100 body-motion clips and 41,148 augmented hand-motion clips of 120 frames. Pairing produces approximately 17.4M full-body frames; these quantities describe different construction stages. ARCTIC/GRAB test sources and task-specific test conditions are described, but aggregate source-ancestor split grouping is not fully enumerated.
metrics: Trajectory failure percentage, location error, MotionCritic body realism, hand quality/contact/penetration measures and human preference. MotionCritic excludes local hand articulation to match its expected representation.

title: FrankenMotion: Part-level Human Motion Generation and Composition
summary: Learns hierarchical part/action/sequence-conditioned diffusion instead of test-time pose stitching.
method: CLIP action/part embeddings are PCA-reduced to 50 dimensions, expanded framewise and concatenated with noisy motion through an MLP; sequence and diffusion-step features are extra tokens. Unknown labels are zeroed; Beta-distributed random masking improves sparse-conditioning robustness.
conditions: Sequence-level text, action intervals and part-level labels at seven anatomical regions; missing labels are masked. Framewise embeddings and a sequence token supply hierarchical conditions to one diffusion generator.
evaluation: Adapted UniMotion, STMC and DART use a matched pose representation; STMC backbone is retrained on the new annotation pairs. Experiments compare conditioning granularities, missing-input robustness and composing fine-grained part/action controls, with ablations of label/masking strategies.
limitations: LLM annotations and evaluator specialization can bias semantic conclusions. Minute-long generation in one pass is explicitly unsupported. Part-level controllability does not imply natural contact-rich manipulation, and retrained/adapted baselines need the same information contract for fair interpretation.
evidence_locator: Sections 3–4; dataset split paragraph, evaluation protocol and comparison tables; limitations and supplementary label audit.
data_split: FrankenStein extends multi-granularity action/part annotations and divides sequences 80% training, 10% validation and 10% test. The split is not a newly established cross-dataset person-identity split. Fifty manually reviewed annotation samples provide a limited label audit.
metrics: R-Precision and M2T similarity for semantic correctness, FID and diversity for realism. Separate TMR-style evaluators cover seven parts, action level and full sequences; MP-retrieval handles multiple positive captions.

title: Towards Decompositional Human Motion Generation with Energy-Based Diffusion Models
summary: Trains compositional scores to reconstruct holistic motion without individual-concept motion targets.
method: Frozen-VAE motion latents are denoised with summed concept-conditioned predictions (latent-aware), or decomposed cross-attention (semantic-aware). Exp uses decomposed captions; OSS splits text embeddings with orthogonality; SC adds semantic consistency against decomposed embeddings.
conditions: Holistic captions or decomposed concept texts. Explicit decomposition supplies separate text embeddings; orthogonal self-supervision divides latent semantics without external component motion targets, while semantic-consistency supervision uses decomposed caption embeddings.
evaluation: Sections 4.3–4.5 compare latent-aware and semantic-aware formulations, explicit versus self-supervised decomposition and generality across diffusion architectures. Caption-decomposition ablations vary component count; component visualizations inspect disentanglement without treating missing component trajectories as supervised truth.
limitations: Explicit decomposition degrades with three/four texts when source captions lack sufficient details. Semantic disentanglement remains an empirical interpretation, not a physical primitive identity guarantee. Decomposed descriptions and reconstruction scores do not certify object-aware feasibility or causal task order.
evidence_locator: Sections 3.1–3.4, 4.1–4.5; Tables 1–7; Appendices G–I (decomposition/data/metrics).
data_split: HumanML3D and DeCompML support single-caption/compositional tests; MTT evaluates timelines/multiple concepts. DeCompML relabels HumanML3D captions into 87,384 two-sentence groups including mirroring augmentation. Original benchmark partitions are used; a new independently recorded component-motion split is not provided.
metrics: R-Precision, MM-Distance, FID, diversity and multimodality; MTT also uses TMR-Score and transition distance. These assess the recomposed motion, not direct per-primitive ground-truth trajectory recovery.

title: EnergyMoGen: Compositional Human Motion Generation with Energy-Based Diffusion Model in Latent Space
summary: Combines latent and text-attention energy formulations for concept conjunction and negation.
method: Classifier-free diffusion predictions implement latent-aware energy composition. Cross-attention provides semantic-aware composition and adaptive text-embedding gradient updates; Synergistic Energy Fusion reconciles the two. Main inference uses five latent vectors and 50 diffusion steps.
conditions: Multiple textual concepts, including conjunction and negation, applied to a pretrained latent diffusion motion model. Energy-weighted score composition and adaptive cross-attention text updates provide alternative controls whose predictions are fused.
evaluation: Tables compare latent- and skeleton-based generation, latent-aware and semantic-aware energy variants, adaptive gradient descent and synergistic fusion. Main sampling uses five latent vectors and fifty diffusion steps. Supplementary ablations vary guidance weights, latent count and attention-gradient parameters.
limitations: Appendix J shows failure on completely novel concepts. Energy arithmetic is an inference control mechanism, not a physics certificate or independent primitive decomposition. Synthetic augmentation and MTT semantic gains do not establish general object-contact accuracy or causal long-task completion.
evidence_locator: Sections 3–5.4, Tables 1–3; Appendices D–E, I (datasets/metrics), J (limitations).
data_split: HumanML3D uses 80/5/15 training/validation/test percentages. KIT-ML reports processed 4,888/300/830 motions; MTT supplies evaluation-only compositional texts/source motions. Motion VAE and denoising model training precede inference energy composition.
metrics: Standard R-Precision, MM-Distance, FID, diversity and multimodality for single-caption generation; MTT R-Precision, TMR-Score, FID and transition distance evaluate composition and multi-concept synthesis.

title: SINC: Spatial Composition of 3D Human Motions for Simultaneous Action Generation
summary: Studies simultaneous actions through body-part motion composition and synthetic training examples.
limitations: Compatible parts need not preserve balance, scene contacts or object responsibilities. Most experiments focus on action pairs; metric/perceptual mismatch remains. Synthetic source combinations do not automatically provide force-valid or provenance-independent human-object examples.
method: GPT-3 identifies active body parts; body-part motion combinations create synthetic examples for text-to-motion training.
conditions: Two or more simultaneous action descriptions combined as one free-form text. GPT-3 assigns active body parts to source motions; compatible parts are combined into synthetic whole-body examples used alongside real single/pair actions.
evaluation: Tables 2–3 compare single-action generation, direct GPT-guided stitching and training with real/synthetic pairs. Synthetic/real mixing proportions and shared versus separate text encoders are ablated. Real validation pairs evaluate generation beyond merely reconstructing synthetic training outputs. Real and synthetic pairs retain distinct experimental roles throughout the comparison.
data_split: BABEL supplies 2,851 training simultaneous motions and 1,232 validation motions. Removing redundant stand labels and action pairs seen in training yields 667 evaluation sequences. Also uses 24,066/8,711 single-action train/validation segments. Validation is explicitly used as test, not an independent third partition.
metrics: Average Positional Error APE, Average Variance Error AVE and TEMOS motion-embedding score. Body-part assignment accuracy is separately assessed against human yes/no labels, ignoring optional-part ambiguity.
evidence_locator: Sections 3.1–3.3, 4.1–4.6; Tables 1–3; Appendix E evaluation extensions.

title: COSMI: COmpositional Synthesis of Multi-object Interactions
summary: Composes contact-local captured interactions and learns a text-conditioned multi-object diffusion model.
limitations: Sustained concurrent interactions are the target, not dependent multistage activities. Synthetic hours are not independent human capture. Finger precision and contact physics remain limited, and repeated source clips across compositions prevent interpreting holdout as new-person generalization.
method: Transfer interacting body parts with their objects, use mirrored sources, semantic feasibility and geometric rejection; weight-shared object slots implement variable-count diffusion.
conditions: Text, object meshes/names and initial poses for variable numbers of objects. Captured local interaction parts and their associated objects are transferred together; semantic/geometric gates reject unsuitable combinations before text-conditioned diffusion learns the assembled corpus.
evaluation: Tables 2–4 compare one-to-five-object and two-/three-rigid-object tiers with adapted MDM/PriorMDM/HIMO. Generalization is reported per held-out composition/object; slot weighting, text/geometry and guidance ablations examine coordination. Held-out subsets therefore test specific recombinations, not new captured actors.
data_split: Uses composition holdout rather than actor holdout: approximately 187k training and 35k test sequences. Test excludes all black-chair instances and five combinations: walking/apple, sitting/flip-phone, camera/mug, foot-interaction/drinking and standing/water-bottle. Individual component skills remain available in training.
metrics: FID, R-Precision Top-1/3, MM-Distance, diversity, foot sliding, object jerk, temporal/body contact accuracy and frame penetration. Articulated objects add hinge error and sweep; every test sequence has three generations.
evidence_locator: Sections 3–5; Data split/Protocol/Metrics; Tables 2–4; Appendix A split details and evaluator appendix.

title: DuetHOI: Language-Guided Bimanual Hand--Object Motion Generation with Articulation Planning and Contact Refinement
summary: Contact intent and articulation planning condition structured hand/object generation; proximity refinement fixes objects while correcting hands.
limitations: Hand-centric rather than whole-body. Supports one articulation scalar and one instruction, explicitly excluding coupled joints and inter-task transitions. Proximity/physical-plausibility scores are not executed dynamics. StructBiHOI and DuetHOI revisions share one arXiv identity, preventing duplicate-paper counting.
method: ContactVAE samples contact intent; conditional-prior ArtPlanner predicts scalar articulation, ManiVAE compresses hands, and DualFormer couples token/time streams. ProxiRefine corrects hands while fixing generated object motion.
conditions: Language, known object geometry/initial state and sampled contact intent. ArtPlanner produces a scalar articulation reference, while DualFormer couples hand/object tokens; ProxiRefine keeps generated object motion fixed while correcting hand poses.
evaluation: Tables 1–3 compare adapted Text2HOI, LatentHOI and MDM with the same raw task conditions. Ablations remove contact intent, articulation planning, hand compression, stream coordination and object-fixed refinement; per-mode results include unseen-category examples. Unseen-oven evidence is qualitative Figure 5, not an enumerated quantitative category-holdout split.
evidence_locator: Method sections ContactVAE/ArtPlanner/ManiVAE/DualFormer/ProxiRefine; Experiments and Tables 1–3; limitations section.
data_split: ARCTIC tests single/bimanual and rigid/articulated modes; GRAB tests rigid modes. One model trains jointly over available modes, masking absent hands. Main text says baselines share splits but does not enumerate participant partitions/proportions; these are deferred to supplemental protocol rather than independently established here.
metrics: Phy, contact F1, articulated hand MPJPEA, object translation/rotation error OTE/ORE, sample/object diversity SD/OD, contact rate/stability and relative-nearest-neighbor error NN-Rel. Metrics cover geometry, accuracy, diversity and persistence.

title: Surface Keypoint Representation for Multi-Object and Articulated Human-Object Interaction Generation
summary: Represents rigid components with surface-keypoint trajectories, predicts spatiotemporal contact-distance fields and synthesizes contact-guided whole-body motion.
limitations: Remaining floating/penetration and imperfect three-object geometric results remain visible. Inference optimization costs roughly four minutes per 124 frames. Rigid-component point trajectories avoid explicit joint typing but do not guarantee articulation mechanics, grasp forces or dynamic feasibility.
method: Three transformer/flow-matching stages generate rigid-component keypoints, contact-distance fields and body markers; inference optimizes body diffusion noise against contact and object-SDF penetration losses.
conditions: Text and geometry/initial state for rigid components of multiple or articulated objects. Three flow-based stages predict surface keypoints, contact-distance fields and body markers; inference noise optimization enforces surface contact and object-SDF constraints.
evaluation: Tables compare coordinate representations and contact encodings, staged generation and optimization. Extra composition-holdout tests explicitly distinguish individual-object familiarity from unseen combinations; slot permutations test component-order robustness.
evidence_locator: Sections 3.1–3.4, 4.1–4.3; Tables 1–5; Appendix E and Tables 8–10 (held-out compositions/slot order).
data_split: Evaluates ParaHome, HIMO, ARCTIC and OMOMO task settings. ParaHome composition holdout contains 118 two-object and 35 three-object sequences whose object combinations are unseen while each individual object occurs in training. Main benchmark overall partition proportions are not restated.
metrics: FID, R-Precision, diversity, foot sliding, object jerk, temporal/body contact accuracy and SDF penetration. Object-trajectory studies report translation/orientation errors; GT-conditioned OMOMO also reports MPJPE/root error. Codec reconstruction has marker/keypoint error and contact precision/recall.

method: Trajectory diffusion generates human/object paths; action diffusion then conditions densely on these predicted positions. Distal-joint adversarial training and reconstruction guidance target contact and grounded feet.
conditions: Text, human/object initial states, object geometry and desired object goal. Trajectory diffusion predicts intermediate human/object paths; action diffusion conditions on those predictions. Dense future paths are internal outputs, unlike externally supplied waypoint baselines.
evaluation: Tables 1–2 compare CHOIS, HOIFHLI and OMOMO variants. Ablations examine decoupled planning, distal-joint adversarial training and reconstruction guidance; DynaPlan illustrates moving-obstacle adaptation. Appendix B discusses foot-hovering versus sliding and contact-penetration tradeoffs.
limitations: Rigid objects only; DynaPlan uses one manipulated object and one moving obstacle. Guidance has no simulation-based feasibility guarantee. Baselines with true object trajectories consume stronger information and should not be conflated with initial/goal-conditioned generation.
evidence_locator: Sections 3.1–3.3, 4.1–4.5; Tables 1–2; Appendices B–D (metric tradeoffs, guidance, DynaPlan).
title: Decoupled Generative Modeling for Human-Object Interaction Synthesis
summary: DecHOI separates goal-conditioned trajectory planning from contact-oriented action generation.
data_split: FullBodyManipulation supplies approximately ten hours of interaction, with the existing OMOMO partition; 3D-FUTURE supplies unseen furniture shapes. Exact subject counts/proportions are not restated in the inspected setup. Comparisons remove intermediate waypoints from sparse-control baselines to match the harder input setting.
metrics: Start/end object error Ts/Te, foot height/sliding, Top-3 R-Precision, FID, diversity, contact precision/recall/F1/rate, hand/body penetration, MPJPE, root/object translation and object rotation difference.

title: Human-Object Interaction from Human-Level Instructions
summary: Language planning orchestrates contextual full-body manipulation with finger interactions and RL reference tracking.
limitations: Planner-produced future targets are material conditions. Reference-tracking success is not a reference-free policy, and environmental perception remains future work. Multi-stage runtime includes expensive grasp optimization/tracker training; geometry-conditioned generation does not by itself establish broad task autonomy.
method: LLM scene planning and A* navigation feed CoarseNet; predicted contact phases drive grasp generation, wrist-relative RefineNet and FingerNet. RL separately tracks the generated reference.
conditions: Human-level instruction and explicit scene/object geometry/state. LLM scene planning and A* navigation provide target poses/waypoints; contact-phase and grasp synthesis drive coarse/refined body and finger networks. A separate RL policy tracks the generated reference.
evaluation: Section 7 separates scene planning, coarse/refined/finger generation and physics tracking. Tables compare CoarseNet variants and grasp alternatives, including provided contact phases; supplementary navigation testing uses HumanML3D test data. Tracking is an additional trained execution stage.
evidence_locator: Sections 3–6; Sections 7.1–7.4 and Tables 2–3; supplementary implementation/navigation and tracker evaluations.
data_split: Uses FullBodyManipulation for body/object generation, GRAB for finger interactions and HumanML3D for navigation, following standard source partitions. Exact ratios are not enumerated in the main protocol. High-level planner evaluation uses twenty-five designed instructions rather than a learned held-out task split.
metrics: Planner object-position/orientation error rates; waypoint error Txy, foot height/sliding, contact precision/recall/F1, contact coverage, intersection volume, MPJPE and object translation/rotation errors; perceptual preference complements these.

title: PrimHOI: Compositional Human-Object Interaction via Reusable Primitives
summary: Composes relative-geometry interaction primitives spatially and temporally through hierarchical planning, targeting unseen multi-object tasks.
limitations: Hand-designed primitive vocabulary and small designed task battery bound zero-shot claims. Requires known geometry and reliable symbolic preconditions; primitive planning differs from a unified learned sequence generator. Public repository presence does not establish a released runnable implementation.
method: Factors interactions into relative-geometry primitives such as grasp, clamp and support. Symbolic state transitions compose these primitives, geometric optimization builds key poses, and a retrained contact-guided diffusion controller fills temporal intervals while preserving active constraints.
conditions: Task instruction, known objects and relative contact geometry. LLM/PDDL-HOI planning produces subgoal graphs, then primitive contact factors specify key poses and object paths; LocalControl generates intermediate human motion with contact constraints and post-optimization.
evaluation: Tables 1–3 compare direct GPT planning, primitive hints and PDDL-HOI, then IK/ProgMoGen and LocalControl with/without intermediate trajectories and multiple runs. Authors explicitly avoid relying on distribution FID for out-of-distribution multi-object cases.
evidence_locator: Sections 3.1–3.4, 4.1–4.4; Tables 1–3; Appendix B evaluation details.
data_split: Primitive sources mix OMOMO, BEHAVE and analytic support functions; LocalControl retrains on a No-Walk HumanML3D variant. No conventional held-out-task percentage is reported. Planner tests three designed tasks, with five/five/ten trials, distinct from low-level contact-guidance experiments.
metrics: Planner success rate, action-count efficiency and solution diversity. Motion tests report maximum joint acceleration and constraint errors, plus human-rated success/naturality on 1–10 scales. FID/R-Precision/diversity apply only to matched training-data variants.
full_text_version: Proceedings/author PDF as retrieved 2026-11-19; no printed own-paper arXiv version found.

title: HIMO: A New Benchmark for Full-Body Human Interacting with Multiple Objects
summary: Multi-object full-body mocap with text and temporal segments; diffusion branches and autoregressive segments support timeline control.
limitations: Captured interactions cover a bounded set of two/three-object settings. Explicit schedules provide temporal structure; distributional language/HOI scores do not independently certify grasp support, collision-free transitions, causal object-state prerequisites or unseen-person generalization.
method: Dual human/object diffusion branches exchange information through mutual interaction; segmented generation conditions later intervals on preceding motion.
conditions: Text descriptions and two/three object geometries/initial states; the segmented variant additionally consumes explicit interval descriptions and previous generated segment context. Human/object diffusion branches exchange mutual-interaction information.
evaluation: Baseline comparisons distinguish full-sequence HIMO-Gen from autoregressive HIMO-SegGen, with maximum lengths of 300 and 100 frames. Tables assess two-/three-object generation, unseen geometry and timeline composition, plus ablations of cross-branch mutual interaction and segment conditioning. Captured clips, temporal segments and augmented examples retain different counting units.
data_split: HIMO uses train/test/validation proportions 0.8/0.15/0.05. Two-object and three-object partitions are evaluated separately. The paper does not establish source-ancestor or actor-disjoint grouping from these proportions; segmented generation should not be interpreted as a separate independent capture split.
metrics: Contrastively trained joint human-object/text feature R-Precision, MM-Distance, FID, diversity and multimodality. Feature scores measure synchronized human/object distribution and language agreement; additional geometry/motion analyses supplement them.
evidence_locator: Sections 3–4; Section 5 Dataset Details/Evaluation Metrics; Tables 2–4 and supplementary baseline details.

title: Controllable Human-Object Interaction Synthesis
summary: Joint human/object/contact diffusion combines geometry supervision with contact guidance and connects to planning for extended manipulation.
limitations: Future waypoints are required conditioning, not generated task trajectories. Rigid-object scope and kinematic contact guidance limit claims of articulated manipulation or force-valid grasping. Retaining source category trajectories for unseen meshes tests shape adaptation rather than unrestricted new-task discovery.
method: Transformer denoises synchronized human poses, object poses and hand-contact labels; object geometry loss improves waypoint adherence and sampling guidance constrains contacts.
conditions: Object mesh, initial human/object pose, text and sparse future object waypoints. Joint diffusion predicts body/object/contact labels; geometry loss and sampling guidance align motion with waypoints and encourage hand contact.
evaluation: Tables 1–2 compare generation on captured and unseen geometry with object-motion-conditioned and waypoint-driven baselines. Guidance and geometry-loss ablations isolate controllability and contact. Extended scene demonstrations obtain object routes through planning rather than learning task-level navigation from initial state alone. Baseline conditions must distinguish sparse waypoints from full future object trajectories.
data_split: FullBodyManipulation/OMOMO uses fifteen training subjects and two test subjects; vacuum/mop articulated cases are excluded. Seventeen unseen 3D-FUTURE objects test geometry transfer, with waypoints extracted every thirty frames from same-category held-out human-object recordings.
metrics: Start/end/waypoint errors Ts/Te/Txy, foot sliding/height, FID/R-Precision, contact precision/recall/F1 and penetration; GT body/object errors and perceptual preference provide complementary measures.
evidence_locator: Sections 3.1–3.4, 4.1–4.5; Tables 1–2; unseen-object conditions in Section 4.1.

title: Template Free Reconstruction of Human-object Interaction with Procedural Interaction Generation
summary: Procedurally creates varied human-object interaction pairs and trains an image-conditioned reconstruction model for unseen objects.
limitations: Static interaction pairs cannot be reported as motion sequences or hours. Seed contact patterns limit synthesized diversity; heavy occlusion and body-shape ambiguity remain. HDM does not handle multiple humans/objects, and contact-preserving optimization is not a dynamic interaction certificate.
method: Category-specific autoencoder correspondences transfer contacts to replacement objects; joint pose optimization preserves contact and reduces collisions, followed by textured rendering. HDM reconstructs joint then separate human/object point clouds.
conditions: Procedural generator consumes captured interaction seeds and replacement object shapes with category correspondences. HDM reconstruction consumes an RGB image, then predicts joint and separated human/object point clouds without a known test object template.
evaluation: Section 4 compares HDM with interaction reconstruction baselines, procedural training-data variants and joint/separate denoising designs. Real-image tests include unseen categories; supplementary analyses examine data scaling, diffusion refinement and detailed shape fidelity.
evidence_locator: Sections 3.1–3.3, 4.1–4.4; reconstruction result tables; supplementary Sections B–C (ablation/limitations).
data_split: Procigen synthesizes static pairs/images from source interactions rather than temporal clips. Reconstruction is evaluated on captured BEHAVE/InterCap and novel object categories. Exact image train/test percentages are not restated in the main setup; source/category generalization must be distinguished from independent motion splitting.
metrics: Chamfer-distance-based F-score at one-centimeter threshold, separately for human, object and combined point clouds. Dataset-scale and limited-data ablations evaluate reconstruction coverage; shape fidelity is also visualized with reconstructed surfaces.

title: World2HOSI: A Multi-Expert Harness for Long-Horizon Human-Object-Scene Interaction Generation
summary: Orchestrates navigation, object and scene interaction experts around persistent scene state, reconciling boundaries and updating object effects.
limitations: Expert availability and planning assumptions bound transfer. Bounded residual control cannot rescue fundamentally infeasible references; a multi-expert harness is not one unified text-to-motion model or a cross-dataset dataset-construction method.
method: Structured MotionIR and state updates compile expert conditions; incoming-prefix translation/SO(3) offsets decay with quintic smoothstep. Bounded residual RL tracks references and objects move through simulated contacts.
conditions: Human-level instruction, reconstructed/synthetic scene state and available motion experts. MotionIR compiles navigation, object and scene subgoals; state updates carry object effects across stages, while transition alignment and bounded residual RL reconcile executed references.
evaluation: Experiments compare expert orchestration, scene-state maintenance, boundary alignment and physics correction, with failures and component ablations. Later stages receive task-progress credit only after prerequisite stages are observed, making task-order evaluation materially different from endpoint matching.
data_split: Constructs ten ISP scenes and twenty instructions, each run with three random seeds: sixty sequences. This is a designed evaluation suite, not a percentage train/test split. Expert training sources and residual-controller training are separate from the task-level benchmark.
metrics: Waypoint error Txy, ordered task progress St, geometry score Sg, moving-object contact OCP, severe-penetration frame ratio with two-centimeter threshold, non-contact object displacement NCOD and object-scene penetration; body tracking/continuity measurements supplement task outcomes.
evidence_locator: Sections 3–4; Section 4 Dataset and metrics; main comparison/ablation tables; Appendix A.4 scoring rules.

title: Synthesizing Diverse Human Motions in 3D Indoor Scenes
summary: DIMOS uses learned motion primitives and scene-aware policies to navigate and perform successive furniture interactions.
limitations: Policies act in a learned kinematic primitive space, not a torque-level physical humanoid simulator. Mainly static furniture interactions; moving-object manipulation and contact forces are outside scope. Ten novel meshes do not establish arbitrary semantic task-chain generalization.
method: Policies select latent actions of generative motion primitives; navigation uses walkability features and waypoints, interaction uses SDF proximity and marker goals.
conditions: Initial body state, 3D scene geometry, navigation waypoints and target interaction markers. Policies select latent actions of generative motion primitives, using walkability for travel and signed-distance/proximity features for furniture interaction.
evaluation: Section 4 compares locomotion with SAMP/GAMMA and fine-grained static-object interaction with scene-aware alternatives. Combined long demonstrations switch travel and interaction policies, showing sequential navigation followed by goal-conditioned sitting/lying in novel furniture layouts.
data_split: Primitive training uses AMASS sit/lie actions selected through BABEL plus SAMP data, resampled to forty fps. Interaction evaluation uses ten unseen ShapeNet seats: three armchairs, three straight chairs, three sofas and one L-sofa. Exact motion-source train/test percentage is not reported.
metrics: Locomotion completion/time, path and collision measures; target-marker accuracy, penetration/contact and diversity for sitting/lying. Kinematic quality and scene goal completion are evaluated separately from policy reward optimization.
evidence_locator: Sections 3.1–3.3, 4.1–4.3; Tables 1–3; supplementary long-sequence examples.

title: InterMask: 3D Human Interaction Generation via Collaborative Masked Modeling
summary: Collaboratively predicts masked discrete motion tokens for two people and also supports reaction generation.
limitations: Two-person scope does not establish arbitrary actor count or object-state planning. Surface conversion can expose inter-person penetration; fast actions may jerk and dataset dance bias remains. Learned interaction embeddings do not independently validate contact forces or chronological task success.
method: Shared 2D VQ-VAE preserves spatial/temporal tokens; collaborative transformer combines self, spatiotemporal and cross-person attention. Iterative confidence remasking generates both actors jointly.
conditions: Text for joint two-person generation; reaction completion additionally provides one actor motion. A shared spatial-temporal VQ codec represents both people, and a collaborative masked transformer iteratively predicts/remasks tokens with cross-person attention.
evaluation: Tables compare diffusion/autoregressive interaction generators and masked-model variants. Codec reconstruction and attention/masking ablations test whether preserving spatial tokens and communication improves quality. Inference uses iterative confidence-based selection rather than one-pass deterministic stitching.
evidence_locator: Sections 3.1–3.4, 4.1–4.4; main comparison/ablation tables; Appendix E implementation and limitations.
data_split: Evaluates InterHuman and InterX with the corresponding standard dataset protocols. Exact actor/sequence train/validation/test proportions are not restated in the inspected setup. InterX includes richer body/hand representation; its scores should not be merged numerically with InterHuman results.
metrics: Feature FID, R-Precision, MM-Distance, diversity and multimodality using the established interaction evaluators. Reaction-generation and ablation results assess conditional completion in addition to joint text-driven synthesis.

title: InterGen: Diffusion-based Multi-human Motion Generation under Complex Interactions
summary: Two cooperative weight-sharing denoisers exchange mutual attention to generate coordinated two-person motion from text.
limitations: Two-person generation is the demonstrated contract. Skeletal relation losses are not contact dynamics; no persistent manipulated-object state is represented. Mirroring/swapping are data transformations, not new people or independent captures, and feature quality need not imply mesh-level collision freedom.
method: Shared denoisers, mutual attention, world-frame joint representation and spatial-relation regularization with damping preserve interpersonal coordination.
conditions: Text describing a two-person interaction, plus optional partial/prefix controls in applications. Two weight-sharing denoisers use mutual attention; world-frame joints and relation losses preserve relative positions/orientations.
evaluation: Comparisons retrain single-person baselines for two-person output on the same InterHuman training data. ComMDM is additionally reported in its original small-data setup, which is a different training contract. Ablations inspect mutual attention, shared weights, representation and regularization scheduling. The retained world frame preserves the two actors’ relative geometry.
data_split: InterHuman supplies synchronized paired motion and descriptions. Mirroring and person-order swapping augment data; Section 5 follows the HumanML3D partition protocol without printing new percentages there. A cross-person identity-disjoint or independently held-out composition guarantee is not stated.
metrics: R-Precision Top-1/2/3, MM-Distance, FID, diversity and multimodality from joint-interaction/text embeddings. Component studies evaluate spatial relation regularization and coordinated denoising; perceptual evaluation supplements feature scores.
evidence_locator: Sections 3–4 (dataset/model), Section 5 Experiments; quantitative comparison and ablation tables; regularization schedule Eq. 14.

title: ReMoS: 3D Motion-Conditioned Reaction Synthesis for Two-Person Interactions
summary: Spatiotemporal cross-attention generates a second person’s body and hand response to a given actor motion; contributes ReMoCap.
limitations: Given actor trajectories provide substantial future information. Fast contact-heavy sequences can remain spatially misaligned. Novel partnership is not new-person independence, and proximity masks or low joint error do not establish actual contact forces or safe reactive execution.
method: Cascaded diffusion first generates reactive body joints using joint spatiotemporal cross-attention, then hands with proximity-derived interaction masks; reaction/kinematic losses and inference guidance improve alignment.
conditions: Complete actor motion conditions a generated reactor sequence. Cascaded diffusion predicts reactive body and then fingers; proximity-derived hand masks and reaction/kinematic guidance improve correspondence. This conditions on another person rather than generating both freely from text.
evaluation: Section 5 compares InterFormer, MixNMatch, ComMDM, RAIG and adapted interaction generation, with cascade/attention/guidance ablations. ReMoCap provides approximately 2.04 hours, including contact-heavy dance and martial arts; editing applications vary conditioned actor movements.
evidence_locator: Sections 3–5; main quantitative/user-study tables; supplementary Appendix B.1 (dataset preparation/splits).
data_split: ReMoCap Lindy Hop trains on pairs (A,C), (B,D), (B,C) and tests (A,D), so people recur but partnerships differ. Ninjutsu uses roughly 3:1 train/test with twenty-eight test sequences. ExPI trains on (A,B) and tests (C,D) using its common-action protocol.
metrics: MPJPE and MPJVE, body/hand FID, latent diversity and human-rated quality/plausibility. Body-only and detailed-hand benchmarks are distinguished because ExPI lacks finger supervision.

title: ParaHome: Parameterizing Everyday Home Activities Towards 3D Generative Modeling of Human-Object Interactions
summary: Captures full-body, hand, multi-object and articulated-object activity in a home setting, including sequential and concurrent manipulations.
limitations: Single home setup, artificial markers and restricted objects limit transfer. Future object trajectories are a stronger condition than initial-state generation. Interpolated styles do not demonstrate robust unseen skill composition; paper capture totals differ between 207/208 and should retain source-specific wording.
method: New capture system aligns multicamera object tracking with IMU body/glove motion and post-processing. Baselines study text-conditioned body/hand synthesis and transformer object-state-conditioned body synthesis.
conditions: Capture combines multicamera object markers with body IMUs/gloves and calibrated alignment. Generation studies use text for body/hand output or complete future object-state sequences plus initial person-object relation for body motion.
evaluation: Tables 1–3 separate capture-system validation from learned generation experiments. Mixed-data training and latent interpolation demonstrate body/hand representation compatibility; object-state encoder experiments measure how temporal/spatial cues help reconstruct corresponding human movement.
evidence_locator: Sections 3–4 (capture/validation), 5.1–5.2 and Tables 1–3; Section 6 limitations.
data_split: Studio-home recordings provide continuous activities, not independent synthetic skill combinations. Generation compares ParaHome, HumanML3D and evenly mixed training data against unseen mixed-data motions. Exact train/test proportions and participant-grouping units are not specified in the inspected main protocol.
metrics: Camera/object marker coverage, reprojection/alignment errors and temporal jerk; text generation R-Precision, multimodal distance, FID, diversity/multimodality. Object-guided synthesis reports root-centered joints/wrists, global root/joint errors and foot skating.

title: Generating Diverse and Natural 3D Human Motions From Text
summary: Introduces HumanML3D and a stochastic text-to-motion baseline.
limitations: One-to-many captions and evaluator training bias complicate ranking. Shared units/representation alone do not provide scene geometry, object trajectories, compositional labels or physically valid contacts. Future motion is generated, while duration is separately sampled/provided.
method: Samples duration from text, then generates motion snippets with a temporal VAE.
conditions: Natural-language description and sampled output duration. A text-conditioned temporal VAE predicts short movement snippet codes, whose decoder reconstructs continuous joint motion; curriculum training progressively lengthens predicted sequences.
evaluation: Section 5 compares deterministic language-to-motion baselines with adapted stochastic generators. Ablations examine movement codes, length modeling and curriculum choices. The dataset expands semantic coverage and provides a common evaluation representation; its real-motion statistics are reference values, not model successes. Mirrored annotations are derived observations rather than independent source recordings.
data_split: HumanML3D combines 14,616 motions and 44,970 descriptions from AMASS/HumanAct12. Both HumanML3D and KIT-ML use 0.8/0.15/0.05 training/test/validation partitions, with mirrored motion and left/right caption augmentation. These sequence partitions do not establish cross-dataset person deduplication or held-out action combinations.
metrics: Contrastively trained text/motion embeddings provide R-Precision and multimodal distance; FID measures distribution similarity, diversity spans generated motions and multimodality compares different outputs per caption. Human preference complements these learned-feature measures.
evidence_locator: Sections 3–4 (model/data), Section 5 and Table 1; Section 5.1.1 evaluation metrics and baseline tables.
full_text_version: Proceedings/author PDF as retrieved 2026-11-19; no printed own-paper arXiv version found.

title: Perpetual Humanoid Control for Real-time Simulated Avatars
summary: Scales physics-based imitation with recovery from falls and noisy reference motion.
limitations: Consumes privileged future references; success is tracking rather than autonomous generation or task planning. Progressive training is costly, and scene/terrain awareness remains limited. Excluding object interaction prevents interpreting reported rates as human-object contact or loco-manipulation execution accuracy.
method: Progressive multiplicative control allocates capacity for difficult motions and recovery.
conditions: Full future reference motion and simulated humanoid state for imitation; recovery observations handle falls and imperfect upstream pose estimates. Progressive multiplicative control adds capacity for difficult motions without residual external forces.
evaluation: Table 1 compares UHC with/without residual forces on captured trajectories. Further tests assess recovery, noisy poses and real-time upstream reconstruction. Ablations examine primitive capacity and recovery training, showing physics-based imitation as an infrastructure component. Recovery transitions are trained deliberately rather than inferred from imitation success alone.
data_split: High-quality tests contain 11,313 AMASS training, 140 AMASS test and 140 Human3.6M motion sequences after excluding human-object interactions. Additional noisy/image-derived inputs test robustness. These are motion imitation partitions, not a language or compositional action split.
metrics: Imitation success, global/local MPJPE, acceleration/velocity error and recovery behavior. Tables distinguish controllers with residual force control from PHC without it; results average three runs.
evidence_locator: Sections 3.1–3.3, 4.1–4.4; Table 1 and recovery/noisy-input result tables; limitations.

title: Weave: Learning Whole-Body Dexterous Loco-Manipulation from Human-Object Interactions
summary: Contact-aware retargeting and approach completion feed a geometry/contact-aware whole-body and finger controller; releases simulated robot-object rollouts.
limitations: Released simulator rollouts are not hardware recordings. Unseen sequence results use familiar objects and harder generated approach prefixes; they do not demonstrate arbitrary new geometry/tasks. Contact-aware tracking is distinct from generating novel human task sequences.
method: Constructs executable interaction references, then tracks them with coordinated body and finger control.
conditions: Retargeted human-object references, geometry/contact descriptors and simulated robot/object state. Approach completion adds locomotion prefixes before manipulation; coordinated body/finger control tracks expected contacts with local reference information.
evaluation: Compares object specialists and a unified multi-object policy; evaluates train performance, transfer to unseen sequences and an oracle trained directly on test references. Failure/termination checks include positional deviation and lost expected contact for ten control steps. The oracle isolates reference-trackability from generalization of the trained controller.
data_split: Nine-object G1 reference data divide into 7,869 training trajectories (19.56 h) and 1,605 test trajectories (3.67 h). Test sequences use the same objects, with three approach variants per training interaction and five per test interaction, introducing a stated distribution shift.
metrics: Clip-balanced tracking errors, completion success and progress; root/body/finger/object position-orientation measures and contact-related termination. Pooled rates weighted by trajectory count are distinguished from equal-object averages.
evidence_locator: Sections III–IV (reference/control), Section V.A–V.C; Figures 3–5; evaluation metrics and train/test/oracle protocol.

title: Multi-Modal Controlled Coherent Motion Generation
summary: Combines text, speech and trajectory denoisers by body region and recurrently assembles a holistic motion at each diffusion step.
method: Four modality/component denoisers use body masks; a timeline can reassign parts and an LLM can plan intervals.
conditions: Concurrent speech audio, text intervals and optional trajectory. Four component/modality denoisers assign speech to upper-body/facial detail and text to lower body; holistic assembly repeats each diffusion step, with timeline overrides and optional LLM planning.
evaluation: Table 2 compares Weighted Sum, Pseudo-Text and SynTalker. Since baselines cannot accept asynchronous inputs, their text/audio intervals are synchronized. Additional studies test component assembly, trajectory guidance and control overrides, distinguishing benchmark consistency from broad semantic coverage.
limitations: Default fixed part allocation can conflict when text and speech both control upper-body actions. Curated lower-body text and familiar audio-source evaluation do not establish arbitrary cross-modal generalization, object interaction or physically executed gait.
evidence_locator: Sections 3.1–3.4, 4.1–4.4; Table 2; Appendices E/H and extended user-study tables.
data_split: Text training uses the AMASS portion of HumanML3D in SMPL-X; BEAT2 speakers with IDs below ten supply 10.15 training hours. A 1,000-clip test benchmark combines forty lower-body texts and BEAT2 test audio, each with two texts/two neighboring audio clips.
metrics: Text-side FID+, R1 and TMR M2T/M2M; speech-side FID-A, beat consistency and L1 diversity. Five random five-second crops contribute to FID+; human preference measures coherence, timing and instruction following.
